knowledge_point.title: Finding Particular Solutions of Differential Equations by First Rearranging and Then Separating

question.:question/problem:
Find the nonconstant local solution to $y'=2(x + 4)\sqrt{1-y^2}$ by separating variables. Work on a local branch where the sine argument $\theta$ satisfies $-\pi/2<\theta<\pi/2$. Express the solution as $y=\sin(\boxed{\text{expression}}+C)$.

Expression: {{field-1}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2(x + 4)\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2(x + 4)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}y & =\int 2(x + 4)\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{arcsin}⁡y & ={(x + 4)}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

This is a perfectly valid general solution. However, if we want to write $y=y(x)$ explicitly, then we can solve for $y.$ This gives

$$
y=\operatorname{sin}⁡({(x + 4)}^{2}+C)
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

This nonconstant branch applies where $-\pi/2<(x + 4)^2+C<\pi/2$, so $\cos((x + 4)^2+C)>0$. The constant endpoint solutions $y=\pm1$ also solve the ODE.
